source_text: CAPUT VICESIMUM QUINTUM, De mundo. Mundus est compages caeli et hujus terrae omniumque rerum in his pulcherrime intense ordinatarum a DEO Patre per Verbum et Spiritum ipsius ex non apparentibus producta — Hebr. XI.3. Mundus Latinis, Plinio autore, appellatur a perfecta absolutaque elegantia. Hebraeis olam hazzeh, ob initium ab hominum memoria remotum; et Graecis aion — Hebr. XI.3 — non quasi aeternus sit semperque fuerit, sed a stabili ordine rerum, quem Deus in illo firmavit. Item to pan, universum, quod omnes res praeter Deum exsistentes complectatur. Item kosmos propter ornatum et pulchritudinem rerum singularum.
english: The world is the fabric of heaven and this earth and of all things in these most beautifully and intensely ordered, produced by GOD the Father through His Word and Spirit from things not apparent — Hebrews 11:3.

Mundus among the Latins, Pliny being author, is so called from perfect and absolute elegance. Among the Hebrews olam hazzeh, on account of a beginning remote from mens memory; and among the Greeks aion — Hebrews 11:3 — not as if it were eternal and had always been, but from the stable order of things which God established in it. Also to pan, the universe, because it embraces all existing things besides God. Also kosmos on account of the adornment and beauty of singular things.

source_text: Mundus est unus, non plures; finitus, non infinitus; habet principium temporis, non est aeternus. Qui mundum aeternum fingunt cum Aristotele, Scripturae adversantur — Gen. I.1; Psal. XC.2; Joh. XVII.5. Mundus creatus est in tempore, seu cum tempore, non in tempore praeexsistente. Tempus enim mensura est motus creaturarum.
english: The world is one, not many; finite, not infinite; it has a beginning of time, it is not eternal. Those who invent an eternal world with Aristotle oppose Scripture — Genesis 1:1; Psalm 90:2; John 17:5.
The world was created in time, or with time, not in a pre-existing time. For time is the measure of the motion of creatures.

source_text: Mundus in se bonus est — Gen. I.31. Non-ens formaliter est nihilum, effective autem Deus: non quia efficit nihilum, sed quia eo utitur, illudque ordinat ad rerum numerum ac discretionem. Cum enim in rerum productione Deus bonitatis suae divitias ostendat innumeris modis participabiles, neque possit ab una re tota vel totaliter exhauriri, facit res multas, sed ordinatas ad unum, utendo non ente, ut possit multitudo constare. Unde in Deo est una idea sui, quae, quatenus participabilis, est multiplex sine fine. Semper ergo to me on distinguit. Plura, si voles, vide apud Hieron. Zanchium, Zach. Ursinum, Amand. Polanum. Hic enim telam abrumpere cogor. CAPUT VICESIMUM SEXTUM, De iis quae creata sunt in principio, sequitur.
english: The world in itself is good — Genesis 1:31. Non-being formally is nothing, but effectively God: not because He effects nothing, but because He uses it, and orders it to the number and distinction of things.

For since in the production of things God shows the riches of His goodness participable in innumerable ways, and cannot be wholly or totally exhausted by one thing, He makes many things, but ordered to one, by using non-being, that multitude may stand. Hence in God there is one idea of Himself, which, as participable, is multiplex without end. Therefore non-being always distinguishes.

More, if you wish, see in Jerome Zanchi, Zacharias Ursinus, Amandus Polanus. For here I am forced to break off the web. CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX, On those things which were created in the beginning, follows.
